Prepare for a demanding event

Work backwards from the event’s requirements.

Preparation · 5 min read · Updated 2026-11-24

Understand the task

Read the organiser’s current route, distance, time limits, mandatory equipment and load rules. A long distance event and a timed heavy pack event may demand different preparation. Do not assume that every event requires a weighted pack.

Measure your starting point

Choose a repeatable session relevant to the event. Record terrain, load, time and effort. Use the result to identify what needs work: sustained pace, climbing, load comfort, strength or repeated days.

Build and rehearse

Plan progressively harder sessions around enough recovery. Practise the actual equipment and food on a shorter rehearsal. Leave time to adjust before event day; avoid a last-minute jump in load or distance.

Work backwards from a real event

Write down the actual distance, pack requirements, surface, ascent, cut-off and support arrangements. Compare each with a recent repeatable session. Select one gap to address during the next training block. For a multi-day event, include consecutive manageable sessions rather than treating a single fast outing as proof of readiness. Recheck the organiser’s requirements and your progress before committing to harder work.

Balance specificity and strength

Use practice sessions that resemble the demands of your event, but keep other sessions easier and include controlled strength work. A review of military load-carriage training found benefits from combining aerobic and resistance work. That does not turn the study schedule into a requirement for every rucker. Select a training dose you can recover from and revise it when progress stalls.

A practical training week

  1. Set the primary demand first: distance, pace, climbing, load or repeated efforts. Use the organiser rules to decide what to rehearse.
  2. For someone already training regularly, separate a comfortable aerobic session, a controlled strength session and a longer specific outing. Add harder intervals only if recovery is adequate.
  3. Use a representative submaximal rehearsal to check footwear, food, pack stability and pacing. Record elapsed time and how you recover rather than chasing a personal best every week.

Put it into practice

A challenge with different load categories is a reminder to train for the entry you actually choose. Compare the options at Bataan Memorial Death March.

Further reading

  • Knapik and colleagues (2012): physical training and load carriage performance — Systematic review of training interventions, primarily military load carriage.
